citation: Primary (opened): Behzad, Gurney, Wang, Pynadath. 'Beyond Predictions: A Study of AI Strength and Weakness Transparency Communication on Human-AI Collaboration'. arXiv 2508.09033v1, 12 Aug 2025. https://arxiv.org/html/2508.09033v1. Background (not opened in full): Lee & See 2004, 'Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance', Human Factors 46(1):50-80, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1518/hfes.46.1.50_30392. Background: Mehrotra et al., 'A Systematic Review on Fostering Appropriate Trust in Human-AI Interaction', arXiv 2311.06305, Nov 2023.
source_tier: Behzad et al.: preprint (final version slated for Springer LNCS). Lee & See: peer-reviewed, 2004 background. Mehrotra et al.: preprint systematic review, 2023 background.
access_status: Behzad et al.: HTML page fetched and read via summarising fetch tool (substantially read, not verified line by line). Lee & See: abstract and secondary summaries only; full-text PDF mirrors failed (certificate error, course page). Mehrotra et al.: abstract page only; PDF not machine-readable.
sponsor_and_incentive: Behzad et al.: US Army Research Office, Cooperative Agreement W911NF-20-2-0053; academic, no product being sold. Lee & See and Mehrotra: academic, no known sponsor incentive [uncertain].
exact_quotes: Behzad et al., abstract: "conveying AI awareness of its strengths and weaknesses improves trust calibration." Same, abstract: "AI performance insights enhance task performance." Same, discussion: "conveying AI awareness can slightly reduce this blind trust more effectively than simply providing confidence levels." (Quotes taken from the fetch tool's extraction of the page; location is abstract/discussion.) Lee & See abstract (via search result, not full text): "trust guides reliance when complexity and unanticipated situations make a complete understanding of the automation impractical." No verbatim Lee & See passage on calibration/specificity was obtained.
date_and_recency: Behzad et al.: August 2025, within the 12-month window; data collected via Prolific, collection dates not stated in what was read [uncertain]. Lee & See 2004 and Mehrotra 2023 are older background, outside the window.
key_claims: Behzad et al.: telling users how accurate the AI is for cases similar to the current one (a 'self-assessing' explanation) or its confidence improved task performance and trust calibration versus no information; compliance with correct AI advice went up and compliance with wrong-but-overconfident advice was lower with the self-assessing display than with confidence. Lee & See (background, per secondary descriptions): appropriate trust involves calibration, resolution and specificity; this is a conceptual model, not an experiment. Mehrotra (background): review of how appropriate trust is fostered and measured.
headline_figures: Behzad et al. (n=272, ~50 per condition, 40 bonus-eligible tasks, income above/below $80K): mean task score No Helper 0.780, Decision-Only 0.790, 80% Explanation 0.796, Confidence 0.825, Self-Assessing 0.815. Versus control: Confidence +0.045 (p<0.01), Self-Assessing +0.035 (p<0.05); Decision-Only and 80% not significant. Compliance when AI correct (log-odds vs Decision-Only): Self-Assessing 0.803, Confidence 0.721 (p<0.001). Compliance when AI wrong and overconfident: Confidence 1.026 (p<0.01), Self-Assessing 0.632 (p<0.05). Underlying model 80% test accuracy; self-assessing tree 66% accuracy.
sample_unit_and_population: Behzad et al.: 272 US adults on Prolific, mean age 37, 177 female, 185 white; participants as unit; lab-style online task, not engineers, not agents, not software work. Test items were selected to keep the AI at 80% accuracy and to include misleading-confidence cases.
observed_vs_stated: Behzad et al.: compliance and task score are observed behaviour. Self-reported understanding of the AI showed no significant group differences. Lee & See: conceptual.
what_makes_trust_justified: Behzad et al.: showing the user context-specific performance information (accuracy for similar cases) rather than a single overall accuracy figure. Note the 'overall 80% accuracy' condition did not significantly beat control on task score, which is the closest this source gets to a per-task-type vs overall contrast. Lee & See (background): trust should match automation capability, with specificity meaning trust differentiates across functions and contexts [uncertain: exact definitions not verified from full text].
what_it_costs: Behzad et al.: need to build a model that predicts the AI's own errors (a decision tree here) and a display; no human review cost measured. Tracking per-task-type success rates in practice costs logging and sorting task outcomes, which this source does not measure [uncertain].
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance (blind trust in an overconfident wrong AI) and under-reliance.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. In the experiment, the self-assessing display lowered compliance with wrong, overconfident advice (0.632 vs 1.026 for confidence only) in the log-odds comparison.
limitations_stated: Behzad et al.: one task (income prediction), one AI accuracy level (80%), authors call for replication; no self-report differences; awareness-vs-confidence difference slight and not statistically significant; modest 66% self-assessment accuracy; sample skewed female and white, US only. Items were curated, which limits realism.
counter_evidence: Confidence display beat self-assessing display on mean task score (0.825 vs 0.815), so context-specific information did not clearly win. No condition tested trust built up from an observed history of past outcomes by task type; participants got outcome feedback on 40 tasks in all conditions. Lay participants on a toy task, not people supervising coding agents. I did not find in this search any study of LLM coding agents testing per-task-type track records [uncertain: search was brief].
verification_status: Behzad et al. figures and quotes: checked against the arXiv HTML page via fetch tool summary, not independently re-read in full; treat as largely verified, [uncertain] on exact p-value attribution. Lee & See specificity/calibration definitions: NOT verified from primary text [uncertain]. Mehrotra: only abstract confirmed. Search snippets about IJACSA confidence-threshold simulation and Frontiers self-assessment paper (40% trust gain) were not opened [uncertain].
usable_claim: In one 2025 preprint experiment (272 online participants, income prediction), showing people how accurate an AI is for cases like the current one, or its confidence, improved their decisions and reduced following wrong advice more than a single overall accuracy figure. The classic Lee & See framework treats appropriate trust as matched to what automation can actually do, which is consistent with, but does not directly test, setting trust per task type from observed success rates.
do_not_use: Do not say research proves per-task-type track records calibrate trust in coding agents. Do not use the 0.045 or 0.035 score gains as evidence about software work. Do not quote Lee & See definitions of calibration, resolution or specificity until the full text is opened. Do not cite the unopened IJACSA or Frontiers results (84.14%, 40% trust gain).
overlap_with_existing_essays: Unknown: I did not check the Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays [uncertain]. This source concerns trust calibration, not verification, so overlap is likely low.
